items.title: Seven dead and more than 100 injured after trains collide in Egypt
items.summary: Several carriages derailed after two trains travelling in the same direction crashed outside the city of Giza.
items.content:
Figure caption, Footage shows derailed train carriages near Giza in Egypt
At least seven people have died in a train crash near the Egyptian city of Giza, with more than 100 injured.
The country's railway authority said two trains travelling south from Giza and Cairo collided, causing several carriages to derail and fall down an embankment.
Images from the scene showed people looking inside overturned carriages for injured passengers as a massive emergency response was launched.
Egyptian President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi said he had ordered state authorities to "investigate the circumstances of the accident, and hold accountable anyone found to have been negligent".
The public prosecutor's office warned the death toll could rise.
Image caption, Uninjured passengers and passersby searched derailed carriages for injured people
The government said hospitals in the area had been put "on heightened alert" as they dealt with a massive influx of patients.
Egypt's health minister Dr Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said people were being treated for broken bones and head injuries.
The driver of one of the trains was among those who died in the crash, the ministry confirmed.
The first train involved in the crash was travelling from Giza to Fayoum, south of Cairo, when it crashed into the rear of another service heading south from Cairo to Aswan, which was stationary on the tracks.
Images from the scene showed some carriages had overturned, with the body of at least one appearing to have split in two.
Trains between Giza and the Upper Egypt region were suspended as cranes were dispatched to remove the wrecked trains.
The collision occurred in the area between Kafr Ammar and Al-Raqqa stations in Al-Ayyat, close to where Egypt's deadliest train tragedy occurred in February 2002, when a fire engulfed a passenger train travelling from Cairo to Luxor.
The train continued for around nine kilometres (5.6 miles) before coming to a halt.
In that incident, more than 370 people were officially reported killed, although some estimates put the toll considerably higher.
Two further crashes in the area in 2009 killed dozens more.
There were calls in Egypt on Sunday for the transport minister to resign over the latest deadly rail disaster.

Iran Plans to Build 110 Bcm Natural Gas Pipeline with Russia
Iran plans to build a pipeline to import Russian natural gas with a capacity of 110 billion cubic meters (bcm), Iranian Ambassador to Russia Kazem Jalali said on November 7, according to Iranian news website Al-Alam.
Jalali provided details of the project, which were discussed during a recent meeting between Major General Mohsen Rezaei and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
He said the initial phase of the project would have a capacity of 55 bcm, adding that it was expected to be completed within two to three years.
Jalali noted that the general principles of the strategic project had been approved during a trilateral meeting between the presidents of Iran, Russia, and Azerbaijan.
He added that finalizing the gas pricing formula between the National Iranian Gas Company and its Russian counterpart, following Rezaei's talks with Putin, was the last remaining step before the contracts could be implemented.
In the short term, Iran plans to use existing pipelines, although bringing them into operation would require rehabilitation work and trilateral cooperation between Iran, Russia, and Azerbaijan, Jalali said.
He added that a gas-swap arrangement, under which Russia would supply gas to northern Azerbaijan in exchange for equivalent volumes being delivered to Iran from southern Azerbaijan, was being discussed as the fastest viable option.

Lisa Nandy said on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that an ‘honest conversation’ was needed after a decade in which Britons had been badly let down. Photograph: Jeff Overs/PA
Lisa Nandy said on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that an ‘honest conversation’ was needed after a decade in which Britons had been badly let down. Photograph: Jeff Overs/PA
Lisa Nandy wary of ‘circular arguments’ about rejoining EU
Culture secretary pushes back against talk of revisiting Brexit but says closer ties would fulfil referendum promises
One of Andy Burnham’s cabinet ministers has said she wants to avoid “circular arguments” about whether the UK should rejoin the EU, underlining divisions at the top of government over revisiting Brexit .
Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, appeared to suggest she was not in favour of rejoining the trade bloc, but she said the prime minister should still pursue closer ties to fulfil the promises made at the time of the referendum.
She is one of a handful of cabinet ministers who are concerned about Burnham’s plan for an “honest conversation” with the public about Brexit and who are privately warning it could reopen a row that would only benefit Nigel Farage’s Reform UK.
“I do not believe that anybody wants to repeat circular arguments about in or out, leave or remain. I do think, though, that over the last decade we have let the British people down very badly,” she told the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme.
Five European leaders call for closer EU-UK ties ahead of Brussels summit
Nandy, whose Wigan seat voted overwhelmingly for leave in 2016, and who is one of the most cautious in the cabinet about reversing Brexit, was asked if she wanted to go back in. “I don’t know if that’s a choice we have,” she said.
However, she did concede that Burnham was trying to address the failings of the Brexit deal, telling Sky News it was important to “be honest” and highlight that “the deal that we got is not what we were promised”.
The culture secretary stressed there were “trade-offs and choices” to be made which involved a conversation with people across the country, indicating that Brexit would be a key theme of the next election campaign.
Burnham will attend the European Political Community summit in Dublin on Thursday. Downing Street sources said he would use it to get Labour’s reset deal over the line and to meet many European leaders for the first time.
In private, EU counterparts will be expecting Burnham to set out his ambitions for further integration after he announced his intention to move beyond Labour’s “red lines” on the bloc after the next election.
At a Brexit reset meeting on 20 November in Brussels, agreements on agriculture and food, emissions trading and youth experience visas are expected to be confirmed.
Burnham said at the weekend there was more to come. “This summit will show what we can achieve when we work together, but it doesn’t need to be the end of our ambition,” he told the Sunday Mirror.
Officials will also discuss the agenda for the next round of the reset, which could include another attempt for the UK to join the EU’s €150bn (£125bn) Safe defence fund , collaboration on law enforcement and borders, and visas for touring artists.
Soon after the Brussels summit, Burnham is expected to give a speech setting out options for a closer relationship with the EU, arguing it would be in the UK’s long-term interest. No 10 sources said he wanted to “frame the conversation, not go straight to the endgame” before testing public opinion.
Senior government figures say Burnham wants a mandate to start negotiations with the EU in Labour’s next election manifesto, but that any subsequent referendum would be solely confirmatory.
“You can’t ask people to vote on an undefined plan like in 2016. That was David Cameron’s mistake,” one said.
However, Burnham has faced reservations from others within his cabinet. The business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, and home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, are cautious about pushing to fully rejoin.
The EU’s former chief Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier said London could not have the “single market à la carte” by cherrypicking which of the four freedoms – including freedom of movement – it would like in future negotiations.
“There is no cherrypicking. There will be no possibility to have one freedom and not the other,” he told the BBC.
Nandy was forced to reject allegations that celebrating the UK rejoining the Erasmus plus scheme by linking it to Remembrance Sunday was inappropriate, after suggesting it would help to honour “the immense courage of those who served our country” before Remembrance Sunday.
Kevin Hollinrake, the Tory chair, suggested she was using the national civic occasion to “try to make an EU membership pitch”. He said: “Our veterans did not fight for a student exchange scheme.”
Speaking on Sky News, Nandy responded: “They are the only party that is talking about Brexit and the EU. What we are announcing this weekend is that we’re going to widen the Erasmus scheme.

items.summary: China’s zero-tariff offer trumps Washington’s trade blow to SA  Johannesburg Sunday World
items.content:
Dennis Munene | China’s zero-tariff offer trumps Washington’s trade blow to SADennis
China’s trade agreement offers South Africa access to a consumer market size of more than 1.4 billion, one of the largest in the world. / Getty images
The recent announcement by President Donald Trump’s administration that it intends to terminate South Africa’s benefits under the African Growth and Opportunity Act (Agoa), effective January 1, signals Washington’s trade war with Pretoria.
In a rejoinder, South Africa’s Minister of Trade, Parks Tau, said the impact of Trump’s decision, though regrettable, would have a relatively small impact on South Africa’s overall GDP. Historically, the country has been the largest beneficiary of Agoa, exporting about $1.7 billion worth of goods to the US last year.
Agoa-related exports account for about 10% of South Africa’s total exports to the US. When measured against South Africa’s total global exports, they account for only 1%.
Trump’s decision didn’t catch President Cyril Ramaphosa’s administration by surprise.
South Africa’s high-profile genocide case against Israel at the International Court of Justice, the accusation of discrimination against its white minority and land issues have placed Washington and Pretoria on a path of perpetual trade war.
To mitigate the impact of the Agoa fallout, South Africa has pursued new market opportunities across the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), the European Union, India, Asian, the Southern Common Market, the Southern African Development Community, the United Kingdom and China.
Of these, China offers one of the best policy plans to trump Agoa for South Africa.
The zero-tariff policy granted to 53 African countries with diplomatic relations with China, which took effect on May 1, has seen the continent reap big benefits. Trade between China and Africa reached $312.11bn in the first nine months of this year, marking a 22% to 22.3% year-on-year increase according to data from China’s General Administration of Customs.
The zero-tariff has enabled South Africa’s trade with China to reach nearly $15bn from May to August, representing a nearly 24% increase year-on-year. Its agricultural exports to China have surged exponentially to nearly $500 million between May and August, up by more than 35% year-on-year.
The zero-tariff policy offers more benefits to South Africa based on its packaging and its long-term predictability.
First, it comes with respect for sovereignty. China has always adhered to its five principles of peaceful coexistence. The internal affairs of a bilateral sovereign state like South Africa don’t affect its strategic relations.
Second, China’s zero-tariff policy offers South Africa access to a consumer market size of more than 1.4 billion, one of the largest in the world. Agoa offered a market size of only about 349.6 million people. The policy will allow South African products to reach the Chinese market and make Chinese companies more aware of the opportunity to invest in South Africa.
Third, it will revitalise South Africa’s industrialisation, unlock its agricultural potential and strengthen its agro-processing supply chain. South Africa is also poised to attract Chinese investment and enhance extraction in mining, with key minerals such as chrome, magnetite and iron ore gaining more access to China’s vast market.
Fourth, the tariff-free arrangement will drive the growth of local value-added manufacturing and automatically improve livelihoods, create jobs, stabilise employment, boost incomes and enhance public welfare.
This will help solve the conflicts in South Africa with other African countries, ensuring that South Africa becomes a gateway for regional integration.
Fifth, the zero-tariff agreements provide the best platform for China and South Africa to fulfil the implementation of the 2024 Beijing Forum on China-Africa Cooperation 10-point partnership action plan. The tariff-free system will create stronger people-to-people bonds, foster friendship and enable ordinary people to share the benefits of development.
Last but not least, the policy will complement and advance South Africa’s strategic trade framework within the AfCFTA, a flagship project of the African Union’s Agenda 2063.
With South Africa being one of Africa’s non-LDCs (least developed countries) whose preferential zero-tariff rate is scheduled to last for a two-year window ending April 30, 2028, the nation will reap tremendous benefits. Luckily, China’s stable governance system under the Communist Party of China could choose to extend this zero-tariff treatment.

items.title: Risk of Iran war escalation remains high despite Democratic sweep in U.S. midterm elections
items.summary: The U.S. and Iran are on a collision course as tensions in the Middle East simmer.
items.content:
Risk of Iran war escalation remains high despite Democratic election sweep
Crude oil prices sold off this week as investors hoped the Democratic victory in the U.S. midterm elections would force an end to the Iran war.
But tensions remain high in the Middle East, with the Gulf states still bracing for escalation, analysts say.
The Democrats' options are limited until they take control of Congress in January.
And President Donald Trump has reiterated that he will not allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.
80% odds of renewed military attack in Iran, oil risk premium to head higher
The U.S. and Iran are careening toward renewed war despite growing hopes this week that the Democrats' decisive midterm election victory will bring the conflict to an end, analysts say.
Crude oil prices fell more than 16% over the last five trading days after U.S. Vice President JD Vance publicly blamed the Republicans' stinging loss on the war. Vance's remarks raised questions about whether the administration still has support to continue the conflict with Iran.
The Democrats plan to use their comfortable majorities in both chambers of Congress to pass a war powers resolution that demands President Donald Trump end the war. But tensions in the Middle East have not eased since the election, and the Democrats aren't sworn in until January, the analysts say.
"Throughout the week, we were struck by the divergence between deepening escalation concerns in the Gulf and the headline-driven off-ramp optimism of market participants thousands of miles away," Helima Croft, head of global commodity strategy at RBC Capital Markets, told investors in a note Friday.
Late Saturday, U.S. Central Command said it disabled a St. Kitts-flagged ship after the tanker ignored multiple warnings and attempted to leave the region after visiting an Iranian port, according to media reports. Iran state media also reported on explosions on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, as well as several blasts occurring in the port of Jask. CNBC couldn't independently confirm the reports.
Several oil tankers have also come under attack near Oman since the election, killing one seafarer, according to maritime security agencies. Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen continue to fire missiles at neighboring Saudi Arabia.
Meanwhile, the U.S. military buildup continues, with a third carrier strike group en route to the region. The consulting group Rapidan Energy sees an 80% chance that fighting will resume as diplomacy stalls.
Trump told reporters Thursday that he will make a decision soon on whether to attack Iran again.
"I would rather not destroy the rest of the country if possible but maybe I'll have to," Trump said in the Oval Office. "You'll know soon enough."
"We're locked and loaded," the president said. "If we have to do the rest of the Iran thing, we're very much locked in."
'Very good chance' we go back to conflict in Iran, says fmr. WH senior advisor Amos Hochstein
Crude oil prices will vault above $100 a barrel again in response to renewed fighting, said Bob McNally, president of Rapidan and a former energy advisor to President George W. Bush. Brent crude, the international benchmark, traded above $97 on Friday, while U.S. crude was around $90.
"President Donald Trump is determined as a legacy item, almost at all costs, to prevent Iran from getting a nuclear weapon, having them give up their nuclear capabilities," McNally told CNBC's " Squawk Box Asia " on Friday.
"The Iranian regime, on the other hand, is not willing to do it," the analyst said. The escalation dynamic remains in place so long as that core difference between the U.S. and Iran persists, he said.
The risk of war is still alive, especially since Trump no longer faces future elections, said Amos Hochstein, a former energy advisor to President Joe Biden . Gasoline, diesel and jet fuel prices would all surge as a consequence, Hochstein told CNBC's " Power Lunch " Friday.
Tehran has been taunting the Trump administration since the election. The social media account of Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said the "process of the U.S.'s collapse has accelerated" after the midterm results.
And Congress is unlikely to pass a war powers resolution until Democrats take control in January. Trump can veto such a resolution anyway.
The main leverage Congress will have is the power of the purse, Croft said. Government funding expires on Dec. 11, and negotiations for another continuing resolution could drag into 2027, she said. This would give Democrats more leverage when they take power in January, the analyst said.
"Importantly, deferring funding decisions would not immediately constrain Trump's ability to conduct military operations, but could significantly reshape the administration's longer-term funding outlook," Croft told investors.
Trump discussed diplomatic efforts to de-escalate tensions in the region with the emir of Qatar during a Friday phone call, according to Qatar's state news agency .
An unnamed senior Iranian official told Reuters on Thursday that Tehran sent a nuclear proposal to the U.S. through Qatar. Tehran will only discuss the proposal after the U.S. meets its demands, the Iranian official told Reuters.
Trump seemed to dismiss the diplomatic efforts Thursday.
"Iran will never have a nuclear weapon," the president said. "They're not doing anything without our approval. It doesn't make any difference what they're looking at," he said of the diplomatic efforts.

Here are the 2 big things we're watching in the stock market in the week ahead
There's one question on everybody's mind entering the new trading week: Where are artificial intelligence stocks going next? The engine of the four-year-old bull market is coming off a bruising week , sparked by the midterm elections, when gubernatorial candidates who support restrictions on data center development won big in states like Texas and Ohio. Voters across the country also approved local ballot measures that could slow the pace of AI investment and construction. As Jim Cramer made clear at Friday's Annual Meeting , this is a real risk to the future earnings of chipmakers, electrical equipment suppliers and other companies with brimming order books to support the AI buildout. We take it seriously and may need to make further adjustments to our stock portfolio to reduce AI exposure. This headwind didn't blow in from nowhere. It's why we exited Corning in early September and Broadcom in late October , and two months ago initiated positions in the non-tech stocks of Kimberly-Clark and Bank of New York . The upshot after such a whirlwind week for the market? No Club holdings are reporting in the coming days and the economic calendar is also fairly light. Here's a closer look at what to expect: 1. AI earnings: Neocloud CoreWeave's earnings report on Tuesday night will help determine whether the AI trade can regain momentum. Even before the election, we've been paying close attention to CoreWeave's bonds and stock as a barometer for souring investor appetite for AI names. How the market responds to CoreWeave's results and commentary on the conference call could have far-reaching implications. "That's going to be the one," Jim said at the Annual Meeting. "You either believe [CEO Michael Intrator] and you see the stock go up and you realize that the AI trade is on. Or you don't believe Michael and the stock plummets, and it'll be a really bad day. ... CoreWeave is so important. It's insanely important." On Thursday morning, CoreWeave's peer in the neocloud game, Nebius , delivers earnings of its own. And that evening, networking giant Cisco Systems and chipmaking equipment supplier Applied Materials will release quarterly results. Both companies are also cogs in the AI trade, so they're firmly on our radar alongside CoreWeave and Nebius. 2. Inflation and Fed speakers: Inflation — and the Federal Reserve's response to it — will also be front and center this week. The October consumer price index is due out Tuesday morning, followed by the producer price index on Friday. As of Sunday, traders are pricing in 78% odds for a quarter-point hike at the Fed's December meeting, according to the CME FedWatch tool . Hot inflation data will likely prompt the market to price in additional tightening ahead, especially in light of an October jobs report on Friday that illustrated the resilience of the U.S. economy. In addition, a number of central bankers are set to give public remarks throughout the week, and their speeches carry market-moving potential of their own. Consider what happened in the runup to the Fed's October meeting, when New York Fed President John Williams said on Sept. 29 that he saw "no need for urgency" on another hike. The market had been pricing hikes at both the October and December meetings, but that shifted to just one additional hike after Williams' comments hit the tape. So, we need to pay attention to both the inflation reports and all the Fedspeak coming our way. Among them, we'll hear from Fed Governor Christopher Waller on Tuesday and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack on Thursday. Both central bankers are voting members of the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee this year. items.title: The Trump coalition is shattered - what will Republicans do now?
items.summary: Republicans can stick with Trumpism or chart a new path, writes BBC Washington correspondent Daniel Bush.
items.content:
By Daniel Bush ,Â  Washington correspondent Â  and Â  Madeline Halpert
Republicans are in soul-searching mode after the coalition that powered Donald Trump to three straight presidential nominations imploded in spectacular fashion in the 2026 midterms.
The stunning election defeat immediately raised questions about the party's future post-Trump.
But there are no easy answers as Republicans face the choice of doubling down on Trumpism or trying to chart a new path forward in his final years in office.
The depth of the problem was captured by outgoing Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who called the midterms "close to an extinction-level event for Republicans".
Others struck a more optimistic tone. Vice-President JD Vance, who blamed the midterm results on public anger over the war with Iran, argued the party could turn things around. Nevertheless Vance acknowledged the fallout will be messy.
"There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why," Vance said.
The wide range of reactions on the right highlights deep fault lines in the party that formed around Trump's improbable rise to the presidency in 2016 and never really went away.
It's too early to tell which faction will win. But while Republicans are still licking their wounds, the intraparty battle Vance predicted is already under way.
The party must decide whether it will be "centred on one figure, one guy, or on a wider set of ideas like conservatism that can win outside the deepest red places," Rina Shah, a Republican strategist, told the BBC.
Critics on the right - the "Never Trumpers" who opposed his first White House campaign - are pushing for a return to the Republican Party's pre-Trump roots, citing the historic losses around the country on election night.
But simply turning back the clock on Trump will be extremely difficult if not impossible to do.
The party has been wholly transformed during Trump's decade-long reign. Most Republicans have shifted to the right on domestic issues like immigration, and rejected the interventionist foreign policy of the George W Bush era that led to the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.
In Congress, the more moderate establishment wing of the party that disliked Trump from the start has almost entirely disappeared, replaced by conservative Trump backers who echo his nativism and populist rhetoric.
That trend continued this year, as old-guard Republicans like John Cornyn in Texas and Maine's Susan Collins, both of whom clashed with Trump over the years, were voted out of office.
Three days after the election Trump appointed Stephen Miller as his new White House chief of staff , replacing Susie Wiles.
The move signalled Trump has no plans to moderate his policies or message in his remaining years in office. Miller, who had been serving as the president's chief domestic policy adviser, is a longtime Trump aide known for his hardline immigration policies.
With Stephen Miller pick, Trump readies for a battle
One of the architects of the Make America Great Again (Maga) movement, Steve Bannon, predicted a "civil war" in the party after the midterms.
Afterwards, he blamed the Republicans' defeat on the economy and "foreign wars". "I don't think we implemented the Maga programme," he said, calling on Trump to double down on mass deportations.
But other Republican strategists said the midterms were a wake up call for Make America Great Again (Maga) loyalists who want Trump's political movement to outlast his presidency.
"There's still plenty of Maga voters out there who have supported Donald Trump through thick and thin," said Whit Ayres, a Republican strategist.
"But there is also a significant portion of the Republican Party that's non-Maga, and that's a majority now."
Should Republican hopefuls distance themselves from Trump?
The party lost control of the House and Senate, as well as governorships and state legislatures in red states like Texas and Kansas where Democrats had been shut out of power for decades - and where Trump won by double digits when he was on the ballot.
The stunning upsets underscored the fickle nature of political coalitions.
Trump expanded the Republican base in 2024, increasing support with Latinos and younger voters among other key groups. Republicans hailed the gains as a sign of future strength for the party.
Just two years later, the party lost ground with nearly every critical voting bloc. According to a New York Times analysis of voter data, Latino support for Democratic candidates increased by 29 percentage points from 2024-26. Support from young voters 18-29 years old increased by 33 points.
The swings reflected polling ahead of the midterms that found widespread disapproval with Trump's handling of the economy, immigration and the war with Iran.
Image caption, Tuesday night saw Trump's Republicans lose in states they had comfortably held for decades
Democrats also capitalised on a public perception that the Trump family and administration is rife with self-dealing and corruption. The president's focus on the White House ballroom and other Washington construction projects also contributed to a sense among voters that he was more focused on his legacy than addressing affordability issues.
It's a sentiment shared by Benjamin Shrader, the leader of the Young Republicans in Austin, who was still shell-shocked when he spoke to the BBC in Texas the morning after his party was almost wiped out in the state by a Democratic "blue tsunami".
Shrader said Trump was still a "force of nature" when asked to reflect on how the president had used his first public appearance after the results to show off the White House ballroom project.
He hesitated before adding: "I would focus on issues that are not ballrooms, that are not renaming things. I would focus on what matters."
The evidence in the immediate aftermath of the midterms suggests that Republicans could benefit by distancing themselves from Trump ahead of 2028.
Figure caption, With Congress flipped, what does Donald Trump do next?
'Vance was the favourite - now the race is wide open'
Vance tried to thread the needle with his midterm assessment blaming the Iran war and calling for a return to "America First." It was a nuanced critique that broke with Trump on an unpopular war, but embraced a broader political brand that remains popular with the Maga base.
Trump's next moves on Iran will be watched closely by the party for their 2028 implications. An escalation would risk fuelling the concerns voiced by Vance and other "America First" proponents.
In his postmortem statement on X, Vance also echoed the growing calls on the right to reexamine US support for Israel. But he also signalled an openness to making some immigration enforcement changes. That clashes with Miller, a Vance ally who has speared the administration's second-term immigration agenda.
Party strategists said the midterm drubbing complicated Vance's path to the nomination.
"Before this midterm, JD Vance was the odds-on favourite to win the Republican nomination in 2028. After this midterm, the nomination battle is completely wide open," Ayres said.
Potential Trump successors have some time to consider their options, but they'll have to make up their minds relatively soon. Any 2028 presidential hopefuls will face pressure to announce White House bids in the next few months. Some could launch campaigns before the end of the year.
Vance's election analysis was widely interpreted as an unofficial signal of his plans to run. It will likely be a crowded primary field.
Image caption, Both Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are seen as contenders for the 2028 nomination
Other rumoured White House contenders include Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, Florida Governor DeSantis, former US ambassador to the United Nations Nikki Haley and former New Jersey Governor Chris Christie, to name a few.
In the next election cycle, Republican presidential and congressional candidates alike will have tough decisions to make on key issues of the day, from US support for Israel to tariffs to the AI boom.
Trump's power may be diminished as he enters the final two years of his second term, but he'll still have the loudest voice in the party over the next two years. It's unclear whether he will get deeply involved in the process or take a hands-off approach.
Trump has praised Vance and Rubio at different times, but typically deflects questions about who he'd like to see succeed him.
His endorsement will loom as the biggest wildcard in the 2028 Republican primary race.
"It remains to be seen who will jump into that race," Ayres said.
"But I think it's going to be a lot larger and more diverse than we anticipated before the midterm election."
Figure caption, 'Hopefully things get done': Americans react to historic political shift

items.title: 'Flat', 'tired', 'cynical': Unusually gloomy Kiwis deliver New Zealand's tightest election in years
items.summary: The national mood is low, and faith in politics even lower - with voters deserting the major parties at the polls.
items.content:
Figure caption, New Zealand election 'too close to call' - so who's won?
New Zealand voted in a new government as fog choked the capital, Wellington, on Saturday - and the mood was as palpable as the grey weather.
"It's pretty flat," 21-year-old Imogen Vlutger says. "There's this kind of apathy and a bit of dread."
"Tired. I think we're all tired," Symone, 28, admits.
"I didn't even vote," one man in his 40s sheepishly confesses. He couldn't bring himself to tick any of the boxes, he explains, declining to chat further.
"Wellington's a bit of a bubble," another voter says, expressing a caveat I heard often, before describing feeling disillusioned.
But polling shows this is a pervasive sentiment across the country: the national mood is low and faith in politics is even lower.
More than half the country no longer sees it as a land of opportunity, a recent study found, while a similar portion fears that the future looks even worse.
Many Kiwis feel the economy is in ruins, there are no jobs, the cost of living has become sky high, the sense of community that used to be a source of national pride is breaking down and there's no sense of genuine progress on policy solutions.
A record number of them are abandoning ship in search of brighter futures elsewhere.
Saturday's election also saw a record number of voters desert the two major parties, giving neither a clear mandate.
But it brought new highs for parties across the spectrum: the left-leaning Greens, the right-wing libertarian Act Party and the centrist Opportunity Party â the latter of which had never won a seat in parliament before but could now hold the balance of power with seven.
Image caption, The Opportunity Party says it is willing to work with either of the major parties
"You have voted to change New Zealand politics for good," the party's ecstatic leader Quilae Wong told Kiwis on election night. "I personally came into this because I was frustrated at the slow pace of change."
It will likely be weeks before we know exactly who will make up the governing coalition and what deals have been made to form it.
But this is only the first of many challenges facing whoever is the next prime minister of a country at a crossroads.
For a long time, the country was viewed as a land of milk and honey â literally â for those who worked hard, with its people ranking amongst the most positive in the world.
A satisfying career, access to quality healthcare, and a close network of family and friends â which research suggests are the three most important building blocks of a happy life â were all there for the taking, University of Auckland Prof Robert MacCulloch says.
"The lifestyle was good," the world-leader in the study of happiness economics tells the BBC. "You weren't the highest paid, but you could get by nicely."
Image caption, Many young people like Michael Dawson (left) feel like they can't get ahead
Many who spoke to the BBC said the country's decline accelerated into a dive during the Covid pandemic.
Unemployment is now at an 11-year high and rising. For Kiwis aged under 24, things haven't been this bad in three decades: jobs are so scarce that one in three either cannot get enough work or have none at all.
Michael Dawson says he did everything he thought he was supposed to: finished school, studied a trade and obtained a qualification, and has applied for dozens of jobs.
But it's been a year now and the job market is so dire he hasn't had a single interview.
"It has sucked. A lot... I'm somewhat cynical with the way I think [about the future] now," the 20-year-old says.
Zainab Ali, chief executive of support service Youth Inspire, has never seen demand so high, with waitlists for its employment aid workshops stretching into the hundreds.
The young people who do make it through their doors on the outskirts of Wellington are disheartened.
"The things we used to hear from everyone's grumpy uncle around the Christmas table sometimes, our young people are now starting to give us that same feedback: like, 'What's the point?'"
Image caption, Sam says he's flirted with a move to Australia
Meanwhile, household electricity bills have jumped drastically, partly driven by global supply shocks. New Zealand remains one of the least affordable places on Earth to rent or buy a home. High inflation means every dollar is having to stretch further.
The island nation produces enough food to feed its population eight times over, but about a quarter of adults are skipping meals because the price of groceries â set by a supermarket duopoly â is among the highest in the developed world.
And the headlines are full of healthcare crises: long waiting lists, chronic understaffing, crumbling health infrastructure and climbing costs for patients. Few stories have captured the state of the system like the death of a man who collapsed in an emergency department toilet after a nine-hour wait in July.
"There's a segment of the population that are facing real material hardship... and then there's another segment of New Zealanders that are quite anxious that they could be next," political scientist Luke Oldfield, from Victoria University of Wellington, says.
Increasingly polarised public debate â around topics like MÄori rights and the Treaty of Waitangi, healthcare for LGBT+ people and immigration â have added to the mental load for many in those communities.
"There's been a few groups feeling like they're being used as a political football," Dr Lara Greaves, who studies Indigenous politics, says.
This perfect storm is driving about 180 people to leave the country every day â a record-breaking exodus that is dividing families, shrinking communities and draining talent pools.
Siblings Sam and Emily tell the BBC that they love New Zealand but find it hard to keep finding reasons to stay. Their friends are leaving en masse and even their parents have considered moving to Australia.
"It's not just that you're being rewarded for going to Australia, it's that you're kind of actively being punished for staying here," Sam says.
Image caption, Stu thinks New Zealand is on its way back up
There are still large parts of the country that feel differently, though.
At the nation's largest livestock saleyard in the town of Feilding, where farmers from all over the island have gathered, Stu Morton says the last year was the best he's had in his 30-year career.
The agriculture industry - which makes up about 3% of New Zealand's GDP - was struggling under the previous Labour government's emissions reductions scheme, he adds, but has turned a corner under the National Party.
He believes the rest of the economy will follow suit.
"We've been through those times where you're questioning 'Where's the future?'
"What helps is having a stable government... [and] it comes down to a positive attitude - appreciating that what you've got is actually okay."
Many of these issues affecting New Zealand are global trends - and it's undeniable that Kiwis' standard of living is better than many others.
But these issues are having a corrosive impact on its national identity.
"It leads to a crisis of confidence about what New Zealand is and where it's going," Helen Clark, who was prime minister from 1999 to 2008, tells the BBC.
Her foundation surveys New Zealanders every year about social cohesion, and its most recent report found Kiwis - in particular young people - feel far more isolated than they did a generation ago, attitudes towards multiculturalism are souring and the population is becoming less hopeful.
Faith in institutions and leaders has taken an alarming turn: only two out of five New Zealanders trust the government to do the right thing, while less than half of the country trusts the courts.
"There's a feeling that, really, there's no-one who cares," Clark says.
Image caption, National Party leader Christopher Luxon is seeking a second term
The transformation former Labour prime minister Jacinda Ardern promised on issues like healthcare and housing when she was elected in 2017 never eventuated. Many other achievements - for example world leading smoking reforms, emissions reduction policies or MÄori language initiatives - have been wound back by her successors.
Her legacy is dominated by polarising Covid decisions, as is Chris Hipkins', who was health minister before his eight months in the top job after Ardern's resignation .
The National Party came to power in 2023 promising to "get our country back on track" and rebuild the economy.
"You'd have to say they've had very limited success," political commentator Grant Duncan says. "And the Luxon government can only blame the previous government for so long."
National delivered the education overhaul it pledged, but the biggest moment of their tenure was the massive hikoi â protest march â led by MÄori over their coalition partner's unpopular bill to redefine the Treaty of Waitangi. And then came the two leadership challenges Christopher Luxon fought off in the past six months.
Image caption, Former PM Chris Hipkins has been leader of New Zealand's centre-left Labour Party since January 2023
There's a sense Labour had too much ambition, much of it costly and unfulfilled, while National doesn't have enough, having spent much of its time and effort wrangling their own flank.
Both governments say their plans for the country were stymied by crises out of their control â such as Covid, the Iran war and US trade antagonism.
But Duncan says that's not cutting it with voters. He's never seen the country quite like this before: "Neither of the parties has been able to field a really strong, inspiring leader. Both of them have a track record of disappointing results."
No matter who ends up taking the top job, Sam says he's not convinced much will change.
"It does just feel stale... a lot of the population probably feels like we could do a bit better," he says. With a wry smile, he adds: "I don't think it helps that they're two white guys named Chris."

items.title: “One War at a Time”: President Abraham Lincoln and the 1861 Trent Affair - Council on Foreign Relations
items.summary: “One War at a Time”: President Abraham Lincoln and the 1861 Trent Affair  Council on Foreign Relations
items.content:
Mary and David Boies Distinguished Senior Fellow in U.S. Foreign Policy
When confronted with a problem, step one should be to avoid making it worse. President Abraham Lincoln followed this advice during the  Trent  affair , a diplomatic crisis between the United States and Great Britain that began 165 years ago today and nearly led to a third Anglo-American war.
When the American Civil War began, Great Britain, France, and other European nations quickly declared neutrality. They granted the Confederacy the status of a “belligerent power” but stopped short of full diplomatic recognition. This decision angered Confederate leaders, who had expected that their monopoly on cotton production would bring European countries to their side. The Union in turn bristled at the decision to grant the South belligerent status; it gave Confederate ships the legal right to under international maritime law to call on neutral ports, to buy weapons, and to attack Union shipping. U.S. officials repeatedly warned Europe that its civil war was strictly an internal affair.
The Confederate July 1861 victory at the Battle of Bull Run, the first major Civil War battle, convinced Confederate President Jefferson Davis that Europe might be willing to extend full diplomatic recognition to the South. He dispatched James Murray Mason and John Slidell to Britain and France to push the case for recognition. In October, Mason and Slidell evaded the Union naval blockade of Charleston, South Carolina, and sailed for Havana, Cuba. There they transferred to the British mail steamer, the RMS Trent , expecting to enjoy safe passage to London under a neutral flag.
Confederate envoys James Murray Mason (left) and John Slidell (right). Wikimedia Commons
Mason and Slidell might have made it London as they planned if not for Captain Charles Wilkes. He was a U.S. naval officer who combined considerable skill with eccentric behavior. The historian George C. Herring described him as follows:
An accomplished scientist as well as naval officer, Wilkes had headed the Great United States Exploring Expedition on its worldwide journey in the 1840s. Arrogant, overbearing, as paranoid as the legendary Capt. William Bligh, he was also impulsive and ambitious—he once promoted himself to captain while at sea and ostentatiously donned the uniform he had packed for the occasion.
Wilkes assumed command of the USS San Jacinto in August 1861. The ship had been patrolling the coast of West Africa as part of the effort to suppress the transatlantic slave trade. But the San Jacinto soon set sail back to North America and began pursuing a Confederate ship that was raiding Union merchant vessels in the Caribbean.
Captain Charles Wilkes, commander of the USS San Jacinto. Smithsonian Museum
While in port in Cuba to replenish the San Jacinto ’s coal supplies, Wilkes learned that Mason and Slidell were traveling on the Trent . Acting without authorization from Washington, Wilkes decided to pursue the British ship. On November 8, the San Jacinto intercepted the much smaller Trent in the Bahamas Channel north of Cuba. Two warning shots persuaded the British captain to allow Union sailors to board his vessel. They seized Mason and Slidell and then allowed the Trent to continue its journey.
The question was what right Wilkes had to board and search a vessel of a foreign nation not at war with the United States. Wilkes, who was not trained as a lawyer, justified the interception to the Trent ’s furious captain on the grounds that Mason and Slidell constituted “contraband,” making their seizure fair game. It was a legal interpretation without precedent. Making matters worse, Wilkes did not bring the Trent itself into port, as required by international law, to have a prize court adjudicate his decision to remove the envoys. He ignored established legal procedure because transferring sailors to man the Trent would have left the San Jacinto dangerously understaffed.
When the news of Mason and Slidell’s capture reached the North, Congress and the public hailed Wilkes as a hero. The New York Times even suggested that the United States “consecrate another Fourth of July” in his honor. Some Union officials privately doubted the legality of Wilkes’s action, but Northerners were looking for a reason to celebrate. Union forces had suffered a string of defeats on the battlefield, dashing hopes of a quick victory. Armed with a memory of two wars with Britain and numerous territorial disputes, many Northerners also doubted that London intended to abide by its pledge not to the rebellion.
The reaction in Britain was the exact opposite. The government and public denounced Wilkes’s interception of a neutral ship travelling between neutral ports as a blatant violation of maritime law. Foreign Secretary Lord John Russell raged that “the world is disgusted by the insolence of the American Republic.”
An article from the Illustrated London News discussing the Trent Affair, December 14, 1861. National Gallery
London demanded Mason and Slidell’s release as well as a formal apology from the Lincoln administration for the Union’s insult to the British flag, or it would break relations with the United States. Such a step typically prefaced a move toward war. To prepare for that possibility, Britain put the Royal Navy on alert, sent 11,000 additional troops to Canada, and began preparing plans to break the Union naval blockade of the Confederacy. France announced that it would support Britain in a war against the United States.
Despite the bellicose posturing, neither the United States nor Britain were eager for war. But neither wanted to back down and lose diplomatic face. For a moment, war seemed certain. But astute diplomacy, the passage of time, and other events cooled the fiery hot passions and allowed calmer heads to prevail.
As London was formulating its ultimatum to Washington, Queen Victoria’s husband and closest advisor, Prince Albert, intervened to persuade the British cabinet to tone done its rhetoric. The softening of London’s language gave Lincoln more freedom to respond to British demands than he otherwise might have had. The exchange of notes between the two capitals took time and allowed leaders on both sides of the Atlantic to assess the true costs of the war. Prince Albert’s death in mid-December after a lengthy illness eclipsed the news of the Trent affair and ushered in a period of national mourning in Britain.
“Albert, Prince Consort,” by John Philip, 1859. Aberdeen Collections
Lincoln recognized early on that war with Britian over the Trent affair would likely cost the Union victory in the Civil War. His war strategy hinged on mobilizing the North’s superior industrial capacities, fighting battles on Confederate territory, and maintaining a naval blockade that deprived the South of trade and war materiel. War with Britain would likely mean a land attack from Canada, threatening the Northern economy and forcing the Union to divert forces from the fight with the Confederacy. The British Navy would also seek to break the Union naval blockade of the South, allowing the Confederacy to trade cotton for weapons, while disrupting maritime commerce in the North, sending its economy into a tailspin.
“Scott’s Anaconda Plan,” by J.B. Elliot, a cartoon map illustrating Union General Winfield Scott’s plan to defeat the Confederacy with a naval blockade, December 1861. Library of Congress
Faced with those facts, Lincoln decided , as he tersely put it: “One war at a time.” On December 26, his cabinet unanimously agreed to release Mason and Slidell. In the note to the British announcing the news, Secretary of State William Seward did not concede that Wilkes had erred in boarding the Trent or in taking the Confederate envoys prisoner. Seward instead argued that Wilkes’s failure to take the Trent to a prize court as dictated by international law obliged their release.
A Harper’s Weekly sketch of President Abraham Lincoln’s cabinet, depicting Secretary of State William Seward standing above Lincoln, July 13, 1861. Smithsonian Design Museum
In a bit of diplomatic chutzpah, Seward also commended Britain on the position it had taken on the Trent affair. In doing so, he argued, London had accepted the longstanding U.S. position on rights of neutral nations to conduct trade unbothered by belligerent nations, a position that Britain had resisted for decades and that had sparked the War of 1812 . This diplomatic victory, many Northerners seemed to agree , was more important than the release of two Confederate envoys.
Happy they had forced the release of Mason and Slidell and avoided war, British leaders pocketed their victory and ignored Seward’s provocation. The two Confederate envoys eventually reached Europe. They failed, however, to win diplomatic recognition for the Confederacy.
“The Great Surrender,” depicting Secretary of State William Seward, with an eagle, setting Mason and Slidell free to British Foreign Secretary John Russell, with a lion, January 1862. Library of Congress
As the Civil War continued, Lincoln faced other foreign policy crises, including further disputes with Britain and a French military intervention in Mexico. But he stuck to his decision to tackle one problem at a time and focused the Union effort on defeating the Confederacy. It was a winning strategy.
Lincoln’s restraint and discipline offer a valuable lesson: The conflicts you avoid can be as important as the ones you wage.
